content.title: About
content.content: Oatmeal consists of whole oat grains that have been steamed and rolled into flat flakes. It is commonly used for breakfast, baking, and cooking. Oatmeal has a mild nutty flavor and a soft texture once prepared.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 5,000 years.
Oat flakes come in “quick‑cooking” (thin) or “old‑fashioned” (thick) varieties.
Oats belong to the grass family and are more closely related to wheat than to rice.
Whole oat kernels contain bran, which is rich in fiber and beta‑glucans.
In some regions oats are also used as animal feed, but food‑grade oats are cleaned to remove gluten contamination.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans help lower cholesterol and support heart health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Oatmeal provides sustained energy and stabilizes blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin B1
items.content: Thiamine (B1) is essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: High in minerals
items.content: Oats supply magnesium, iron, and zinc, important for muscle and immune function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in oats promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats or oat proteins.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Although oats are naturally gluten‑free, they are often processed alongside wheat; people with celiac disease need certified gluten‑free oats.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting oats lowers its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook oatmeal in water or milk, blend into smoothies, stir into yogurt, or use in cookies, muffins, and bread. For quick oats, pour hot liquid over the flakes and let sit 2–3 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store oatmeal in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.
